item.text: {"debateNumber":219,"decisions":[{"moveId":"expected-world-evidence-of-absence","label":"Appeal to authority","type":"fallacy","decision":"rejected","rationale":"Naming Victor Stenger and identifying him as a physicist does not make his status the reason the conclusion should be accepted; Shermer states Stenger’s expectation-based argument, albeit incompletely. The assessment’s material criticism is that no expected condition, failed observation, discriminating prediction, or relevant conception of God is specified. That is missing warrant and precision, not reliance on authority as settling the dispute.","url":"https://logfall.com/fallacies/appeal-to-authority/","context":"Shermer attributes to physicist Victor Stenger the claim that a real God would make the world observably different and that unmet expectations would count against God’s existence."},{"moveId":"believer-bears-proof-burden","label":"Argument from ignorance","type":"fallacy","decision":"rejected","rationale":"Allocating the burden of justification to the person asserting God’s existence permits withholding belief; it does not establish that God is nonexistent or imaginary merely because existence has not been proved. The assessment expressly says an unmet obligation alone does not establish human invention and faults Shermer for not evaluating the available evidence. That is an incomplete motion-level inference, not the catalog’s truth-from-nonproof fallacy.","url":"https://logfall.com/fallacies/argument-from-ignorance/","context":"Shermer says believers must prove God’s existence or explain why belief is justified, while skeptics are not responsible for disproving God before withholding assent."},{"moveId":"believer-bears-proof-burden","label":"Equivocation","type":"fallacy","decision":"rejected","rationale":"The wording juxtaposes two different possible burdens—proving God’s existence and explaining why one believes—but it does not shift the meaning of a single key term during an inference so as to make the conclusion appear stronger. The assessment identifies differing standards and resulting imprecision, not a semantic substitution that carries the reasoning. Treating that underdefined disjunction as equivocation would exceed the exact definition.","url":"https://logfall.com/fallacies/equivocation/","context":"In assigning believers the burden, Shermer says they must either prove God exists or convince listeners why they believe, contrasting both with a skeptic’s burden to disprove God."},{"moveId":"ultimate-beliefs-beyond-proof","label":"Special pleading","type":"fallacy","decision":"accepted","rationale":"McGrath assigns meaning-conferring beliefs a protected evidential category beyond the proof applicable to supposedly shallow truths, while offering no principle showing why importance or existential depth warrants that exception. The assessment makes this materially central: it calls the division unsupported, notes that significance is not connected to evidential status, and warns that the commitments risk insulation from scrutiny. This exactly applies an unjustified different standard.","url":"https://logfall.com/fallacies/special-pleading/","context":"McGrath distinguishes provable “shallow truths” from greater beliefs that supply meaning, purpose, and value, placing the latter beyond proof."},{"moveId":"scientific-theories-change","label":"Argument from ignorance","type":"fallacy","decision":"rejected","rationale":"The move concludes that future scientific conclusions are unknown and present judgments revisable; it does not conclude that Christianity is true because science has not disproved it. The assessment criticizes the failure to connect revisability with present unreliability or increased probability for Christianity. That missing positive connection is underdevelopment and limited relevance, not treating lack of disproof as proof of the contrary claim.","url":"https://logfall.com/fallacies/argument-from-ignorance/","context":"McGrath cites the replacement of an earlier cosmological consensus to argue that current scientific conclusions cannot determine with certainty what investigators will believe a century later."},{"moveId":"many-gods-one-further","label":"Base-rate neglect","type":"bias","decision":"rejected","rationale":"Shermer’s counting argument inadequately translates religious multiplicity into comparative probability, but it does not underweight an identified general background rate in favor of a vivid local case. Indeed, the large cross-cultural count is itself presented as background information. The assessment’s material defect is the unsupported assumption that rival religions are evidentially symmetrical and that their number determines probability, not neglect of a supplied base rate or prior probability.","url":"https://cogbias.site/biases/base-rate-neglect/","context":"Shermer lists numerous historical gods and religions, asks how Yahweh could uniquely be true, and says skeptics merely extend believers’ rejection of rival gods by one more deity."},{"moveId":"science-and-faith-enrich","label":"Subjective validation","type":"bias","decision":"rejected","rationale":"McGrath explicitly reports that faith enriched the significance of his scientific work, so personal meaning is the proposition being asserted rather than evidence offered for that proposition’s external accuracy. The assessment notes that usefulness does not establish truth, but also says the inference from enrichment to God’s reality remains unstated. Because the move does not materially make private resonance the reason Christianity is accurate, the exact bias is not established.","url":"https://cogbias.site/biases/subjective-validation/","context":"McGrath describes faith and science as complementary, saying his religious way of seeing things gave science new significance and enriched his understanding of scientific inquiry."},{"moveId":"recurring-resurrection-myths","label":"Appeal to authority","type":"fallacy","decision":"rejected","rationale":"The passing invitation to think of Joseph Campbell functions as shorthand for comparative mythology, not as a claim that Campbell’s status settles the recurrence or origin of resurrection stories. Shermer supplies his own proposed mechanisms—diffusion and independent creation—though without adequate corroboration or controlled comparison. The assessment locates the material weakness in chronology, resemblance, causal inference, and alternative explanations, not in deference to Campbell’s authority.","url":"https://logfall.com/fallacies/appeal-to-authority/","context":"Shermer invokes pre-Christian resurrection narratives, recurring mythic themes, diffusion, independent invention, and a brief Joseph Campbell reference to propose human origins for parallel stories."},{"moveId":"comparative-worldviews-break-bubble","label":"Belief bias","type":"bias","decision":"rejected","rationale":"Shermer’s reassessment may be evidentially insufficient, but he does not judge a formal argument valid or invalid merely because its conclusion feels believable. He instead treats equally confident, meaningful rival commitments as evidence against inferring unique truth from commitment alone. The assessment faults the jump from equal conviction to equal warrant and from personal reassessment to external falsity. Those are comparative-evidence gaps, not conclusion-believability substituting for evaluation of inference.","url":"https://cogbias.site/biases/belief-bias/","context":"After encountering unfamiliar people who were just as committed to meaning-giving worldviews, Shermer concluded that his former Christianity was something he happened to believe rather than uniquely true."},{"moveId":"comparative-worldviews-break-bubble","label":"Subjective validation","type":"bias","decision":"rejected","rationale":"The autobiographical encounter explains Shermer’s loss of confidence, but his stated reason is the existence of equally committed alternative worldviews, not that Christianity’s falsity felt personally resonant or confirmed a private experience. The assessment recognizes the experience as establishing underdetermination while criticizing the unsupported broader conclusion that no worldview is externally true. That is insufficient comparative warrant; inferring the cataloged psychological validation mechanism would go beyond the move and rationale.","url":"https://cogbias.site/biases/subjective-validation/","context":"Shermer recounts personally meeting adherents of unfamiliar yet deeply meaningful worldviews and moving from that comparison to relativizing his own former Christian commitment."},{"moveId":"ungrounded-values-reflect-society","label":"Begging the question","type":"fallacy","decision":"rejected","rationale":"McGrath presumptively characterizes socially produced values as societal prejudice, but the excerpt is largely an undeveloped grounding question and does not embed the desired conclusion—divine or Christian grounding—inside a premise. The assessment criticizes the unproved assumption that critical reflection, evidence, and shared interests cannot correct social values. That is weak support and imprecise formulation, not a circular argument in which the conclusion has been smuggled into its premises.","url":"https://logfall.com/fallacies/begging-the-question/","context":"McGrath suggests that meaning and value without a firmer basis may merely hypothesize a society’s prejudices and asks what such judgments can actually be based upon."},{"moveId":"secular-values-risk-projection","label":"Special pleading","type":"fallacy","decision":"rejected","rationale":"The move challenges whether naturalistically generated values possess objective stability, but it does not within this excerpt expressly exempt Christian values from a standard that it applies to secular ones. The assessment notes that projection’s possibility does not establish secular instability and that McGrath has not shown transcendent grounding to be available or less projective. Those are missing comparative premises; without an actually applied exemption, they do not satisfy the exact special-pleading definition.","url":"https://logfall.com/fallacies/special-pleading/","context":"McGrath argues that people may project desired or innate preferences into values they then call self-evident, and asks what objective basis prevents that process."},{"moveId":"meaning-available-without-religion","label":"Subjective validation","type":"bias","decision":"rejected","rationale":"Shermer uses reports of scientific and nonreligious meaning to establish that existential fulfillment is available without religion, not to establish that naturalism is true because it feels fulfilling. The assessment carefully distinguishes psychological availability from philosophical adequacy and says the move does not resolve objective grounding. That limitation is underdevelopment relative to McGrath’s challenge, while the exact inference from private resonance to external accuracy is absent.","url":"https://cogbias.site/biases/subjective-validation/","context":"Shermer says scientific understanding can be existentially meaningful and that purpose, meaning, and love can be found both with religion and without it."},{"moveId":"science-does-not-answer-why","label":"Argument from ignorance","type":"fallacy","decision":"rejected","rationale":"McGrath argues only that science does not answer an existential “why” question and that the question should remain open. He does not infer from science’s silence that Christianity’s answer is true. The assessment expressly identifies the missing steps: the move establishes neither that an external answer exists nor that theism provides a warranted answer. Those omissions are incomplete positive argumentation, not truth inferred from a failure to prove or disprove.","url":"https://logfall.com/fallacies/argument-from-ignorance/","context":"McGrath distinguishes science’s account of how humans came to exist from the existential question of why humans are here, which he regards as important despite scientific silence."},{"moveId":"science-does-not-answer-why","label":"Equivocation","type":"fallacy","decision":"rejected","rationale":"The assessment observes that “why” is ambiguous among causal explanation, purpose, and desired significance, but ambiguity alone is not equivocation. In the source, McGrath contrasts science’s causal “how” with an explicitly existential “why”; he does not demonstrably change the meaning of “why” across premises to secure a conclusion. The material defect is failure to specify and defend the explanatory target, not a meaning shift that deceptively strengthens the inference.","url":"https://logfall.com/fallacies/equivocation/","context":"McGrath says science explains how humanity came to be but leaves open the important language of why humanity is here, apparently referring to an existential rather than causal question."},{"moveId":"selective-credit-defies-falsification","label":"Confirmation bias","type":"bias","decision":"rejected","rationale":"The described selective accounting—crediting God for favorable outcomes while withholding blame after unfavorable ones—closely matches confirmation bias, but it is the phenomenon Shermer criticizes, not a defect instantiated by Shermer’s own move. The assessment’s limitation instead faults Shermer for generalizing that practice to believers and for not engaging possible theological distinctions. Because adjudication targets the speaker’s move rather than the criticized behavior, the candidate must be rejected.","url":"https://cogbias.site/biases/confirmation-bias/","context":"Shermer criticizes prayer reasoning in which good outcomes count as divine action while bad outcomes never count against God, making every possible result compatible with belief."},{"moveId":"faith-motivates-relief","label":"Red herring","type":"fallacy","decision":"accepted","rationale":"In response to the evidential problem posed by suffering and apparently absent divine intervention, McGrath turns to the related but less probative point that Christianity condemns suffering and motivates human relief work. The assessment makes the diversion material: it says this does not answer the inference concerning omnipotent intervention, gives responsiveness the weakest dimension, and requires McGrath to explain compatibility between suffering and God’s power. The original challenge therefore remains insufficiently answered.","url":"https://logfall.com/fallacies/red-herring/","context":"McGrath responds to discussion of suffering by emphasizing that Christians regard suffering as wrong and are motivated to enter relief work and medicine to improve the world."},{"moveId":"jesus-claimed-historically-reliable","label":"Begging the question","type":"fallacy","decision":"rejected","rationale":"McGrath asserts belief in the Jesus story’s historical reliability without presenting support, but an unsupported assertion is not automatically circular reasoning. No premise is supplied that restates or covertly assumes historical reliability in order to derive it. The assessment consistently characterizes the defect as absent evidence, an undefended central premise, and failure to compare alternatives. Because it does not identify a conclusion smuggled into premises, the exact definition is unmet.","url":"https://logfall.com/fallacies/begging-the-question/","context":"McGrath states that he believes the Jesus story is historically reliable and deeply significant while openly conceding that he cannot prove the claim."},{"moveId":"jesus-claimed-historically-reliable","label":"Subjective validation","type":"bias","decision":"rejected","rationale":"McGrath places personal belief, historical reliability, and deep significance beside one another, but the excerpt does not state that felt significance is why the story is historically accurate. The assessment says reliability and significance are unsupported and requires McGrath to show why significance supports truth, indicating that the crucial inference is missing rather than materially instantiated. Accepting the bias would infer an unexpressed psychological or causal connection from juxtaposition alone.","url":"https://cogbias.site/biases/subjective-validation/","context":"McGrath personally affirms the Jesus narrative as historically reliable, concedes that he cannot prove it, and immediately describes the narrative as deeply significant."},{"moveId":"old-resurrection-story-insulated","label":"Argument from ignorance","type":"fallacy","decision":"rejected","rationale":"Shermer asks how the resurrection is known and alleges that antiquity permits theological insulation, but he does not conclude in this move that the resurrection is false solely because it has not been proved. The assessment calls this a relevant skeptical challenge while criticizing its failure to examine historical arguments and insulating mechanisms. That is an under-supported challenge to warrant, not the cataloged conversion of nonproof into proof of falsity.","url":"https://logfall.com/fallacies/argument-from-ignorance/","context":"Shermer says the ancient resurrection story can be hidden behind layers of theological argument because it is lost in time, then asks how anyone knows it happened."},{"moveId":"meaning-without-jesus","label":"Subjective validation","type":"bias","decision":"rejected","rationale":"The existential depth attributed to Jewish and Muslim lives is used as a counterexample to the alleged unique necessity of Christianity, not as evidence that Judaism or Islam is externally true. The assessment explicitly limits the result: comparable fulfillment undermines an exclusivity inference but does not adjudicate truth or refute resurrection. Thus the move’s limitation is insufficient comparative evidence for the broader construction thesis, not validation of a truth claim through personal resonance.","url":"https://cogbias.site/biases/subjective-validation/","context":"Shermer points to Jewish and Muslim believers who reject Jesus as savior or resurrected yet possess worldviews he considers equally deep, thoughtful, and purposeful."},{"moveId":"sentient-flourishing-moral-standard","label":"Begging the question","type":"fallacy","decision":"rejected","rationale":"Shermer openly proposes reduced suffering and sentient flourishing as a moral starting point; he does not disguise the desired conclusion inside a premise purporting independently to prove it. The assessment’s normative-bridge criticism establishes that the starting point needs justification and operational rules for conflicts. That is incomplete grounding and underdevelopment, not circularity. No assessment language identifies the moral conclusion as having been covertly assumed in a proof of itself.","url":"https://logfall.com/fallacies/begging-the-question/","context":"Shermer proposes the survival and flourishing of sentient beings as a naturalistic moral baseline and calls actions that lower sentient suffering good."},{"moveId":"morality-needs-beyond-us-framework","label":"Begging the question","type":"fallacy","decision":"rejected","rationale":"McGrath asserts that morality needs a framework beyond individual preference and presents Christianity as a candidate source, but he offers little argument for either proposition. The assessment identifies precisely that unsupported transition: transcendent necessity is asserted, secular alternatives are not refuted, and Christian authority is not established. Mere assertion and missing evidence do not show that the conclusion was embedded in premises, so the circularity required by the definition is absent.","url":"https://logfall.com/fallacies/begging-the-question/","context":"McGrath says moral judgment requires a framework beyond us and adds that Christianity regards human beings as enormously important despite acknowledged problems."},{"moveId":"faith-motivates-good-closing","label":"Subjective validation","type":"bias","decision":"accepted","rationale":"McGrath explicitly moves from what he personally finds in faith—an action-guiding worldview and motivation—to the conclusion that God remains not merely important but valid. That treats private existential and motivational usefulness as support for validity. The assessment identifies this transition as the principal limitation, stating that motivational usefulness does not establish accuracy and requiring a connection from personal experience to reality beyond imagination. The defect is therefore material and exactly definition-matched.","url":"https://cogbias.site/biases/subjective-validation/","context":"In closing, McGrath says faith gives him a way of seeing the world and a desire to act, and that this is why God remains an important and valid idea."}]}
